statement: A rectangular card measures 10 cm by 7 cm. A square of side 3 cm is cut out of one of its corners. What is the perimeter of the shape that is left?

choices.misconception: I added the two new edges from the cut without taking away the two pieces of edge that were removed.
I added all four sides of the cut-out square to the rectangle's perimeter.
I worked out the area that is left, 70 - 9, instead of the perimeter.
I worked out the area of the whole card instead of the perimeter.

hints: Look closely at what happens to the edge at the cut corner.
Cutting a corner square removes two short pieces of the card's edge but adds two new edges of the same lengths. Compare what is lost with what is gained.
The card's perimeter is 2 × (10 + 7) = 34 cm. The cut removes 3 + 3 cm of edge and adds 3 + 3 cm of new edge.

solutions.reliable: The card has perimeter 10 + 7 + 10 + 7 = 34 cm. Cutting a 3 cm square from a corner removes 3 cm from each of two sides, but creates two new edges of 3 cm each, facing inward. The loss and the gain are equal, so the perimeter is still 34 cm. Check by walking around: 10 - 3, then 3, then 3, then 7 - 3, then 10, then 7: 7 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 10 + 7 = 34. The transferable idea: pushing a corner inward keeps every horizontal and vertical length, so the perimeter of a rectilinear shape can stay the same while its area shrinks.
solutions.elegant: Push the two new edges outward back onto the corner: they exactly fill the gap, so the shape has the same perimeter as the full card.

whyOnTest: Perimeter and area are easily confused; cutting a corner changes the area but not the perimeter.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
